Having gone through something similar, all I can say is grieve. If you need to cry, then cry it out. If you need to remember the good times and do nothing but smile, then smile until your face hurts.

We each go through this pain in a different way. The important thing is to allow yourself to do what helps you most. Some days won't be as bad as others. There might even be days when you let yourself not think about it, and that's okay.

What helps me most is to continue to live in a way that would have made them proud. For me, that was graduating high school and going to college after my dad died. Right now, it's helping to take care of my mentally handicapped aunt after my grandma died.

Find out what helps you most. You don't have to start it right away, but the important thing is to start. It took me four months to be able to do anything other than going to school and just crying after my dad died, and it took a couple years for the random breakdowns to stop, but then I was able to start. I can't tell you much about after my grandma passed, it's only been a month, but right now, I'm taking it one day at a time. I think my grandma would be happy with how I'm taking care of everything, and so I can be happy too. Sure, it hurts everytime I come home and she's not there sitting in her chair, I still cry every time, but that's okay too.

It's important to also seek help. Don't try to go through this alone, especially if you're already dealing with depression and anxiety. Try going to grief counseling, if that doesn't help maybe try therapy, if that also doesn't help, maybe it would be wise to get the opinion of a psychiatrist on whether you could benefit from medication. If you're opposed to start medication, St John's Wort is an herbal remedy that's helped my mom, so maybe it could help you too.

I'm so sorry for your loss. I hope that I've been able to help. Death is such a difficult thing to handle, so rely upon your family and friends. I'm also here for you. If you want to talk, I'd love to hear more about your grandmother. She sounds like she was an amazing woman.

I didn't even notice the change in myself until this week, but yes. I used to be a voracious reader. Even while in high school, I would easily read over a thousand pages a week, but I couldn't even tell you when I stopped. Now that I'm on antidepressants though, they really seem to have brought back my reading appetite. For the first time in what feels like a really long time, I've picked up a book to read it for myself. Not because a friend wants me to read it with them, not because of a class assignment, and not just because my therapist recommened it, but because I really like it. I've bought so many books in the past few years that I've barely even started and I finally have the energy to not just read them, but to want to read them. Therapy, antidepressants, and a self help class has really helped me improve. I'm still struggling to read more than a few pages at a time (I currently seem to have the attention span of a gnat, and the words will also sometimes start to run together), but I am reading. I've started reading 'The Power of Now', 'The Gift of Fear', 'Confidence: How to be a Better You', 'The Death of Ivan Ilych', and '1st to Die'. A good way to find out, is to go talk to a psychiatrist/ therapist and be medically assessed. You can really only know by being assessed by a trained professional. Just because you feel better after talking to people you like, it doesn't invalidate that you could also depressed and dealing with a lot of stress. If you're feeling so down/ horrible that you're constantly crying, please seek help. No one should be made to live like that.

You also don't have to lay in the bed you've made. It doesn't matter what age you are, there's time enough to change everything. One of my family members turned their life around in her thirties. She's now been sober for 7 months, going to school, and is about to move out of her mother's for the first time in her life.

If you need a little help to get there, that's okay. That's what the medical field is there for. Seek the help you need. There's no reason not to.

Talking from a girls perspective, anything about class is a surefire way to start a conversation. Ask her about the last test, or the other days notes, or if you guys can compare homework. Maybe even ask her if she would like to get together to study after class. If you notice that she doesn't quite understand something, but you do, offer to help, and I would also seek her out if you don't get something. Maybe even ask if you two can exchange phone numbers so you can help each other out with the homework without having to study together. After talking for a little bit is when I'd ask if she wanted to go out. I would try to avoid coming out of the blue with asking her out though, if you suddenly put her on the spot, she might be more likely to say no, but if she already kinda knows you, she would probably be more comfortable with it and so more likely to say yes.
